transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I guess the thing that finally pushed me to come in is that I’ve been noticing this problem when people are talking to me, especially over at the museum. I’ll be standing there, looking right at somebody while they’re telling me about the next art walk or some detail we’re supposed to remember, and I honestly think I’m listening. I’m not trying to be rude or drift off on purpose.

But then, partway through, I realize I’ve missed the middle of what they said. Like I caught the beginning and maybe the end, but the important part in between is just… gone. Then I have to ask them to run it by me again, and I feel a little embarrassed because they were talking right to my face. It’s been happening enough that I thought maybe I should talk to someone about it.
Do you feel like you’re having trouble hearing what people say?

I don’t think it’s hearing exactly, no. I mean, as far as I can tell, I hear the person’s voice just fine. It’s not like everything sounds muffled, or I’m asking people to speak up because I can’t catch the volume.

It’s more that the words are coming in, but then somehow I don’t hold onto them. Like I’ll hear someone talking, and I know they’re talking to me, but when I go to answer or remember what they said, there’s a gap. So I’m not sure if that counts as “hearing” trouble in the way you mean, but it doesn’t feel like my ears are the problem.
Does this same thing happen when you’re reading something, where you realize you took in the words but didn’t retain what they said?

Yes, that does happen. It’s not every single sentence or anything, but if I sit down with, say, one of those gallery packets or a set of notes from the museum, I’ll start off all right. I’m reading the first paragraph and I think I’m following it.

Then after a few minutes I’ll notice my eyes are still going along the lines, like I’m technically reading the words, but my mind has gone somewhere else. And then I get to the bottom of the page or even just the end of a paragraph and think, “Wait, what did that actually say?” So I have to go back and read the same part again, sometimes more than once. It’s a little frustrating, because it feels like I did the reading, but it didn’t really stick.
Did you have this same kind of trouble focusing when you were a child?

Yes, I think so. Looking back, it wasn’t talked about in the same way then, or at least nobody in my family used any particular name for it, but I remember it being there.

Even in grade school, my report cards would have little comments like “daydreams” or “needs reminders to finish work.” Those kinds of remarks showed up enough that I remember them, not just once. And my mother had to sit beside me when I was doing homework, especially before I was twelve or so, because otherwise I’d just sort of drift off or not finish. She wasn’t doing the work for me, exactly, but she had to keep bringing me back to it and reminding me, “Come on, finish this part,” that kind of thing.

At the time I think everybody just thought I was being slow or not applying myself, but when I think about it now, it feels pretty similar to what I’m describing now, just in a child’s version.
Does this problem with losing track of what people say also happen in other parts of your life outside the museum?

Yes, it does, although the museum is where I notice it the most because people are giving me little bits of information I’m supposed to remember. Like someone will be talking right to me about the next art walk — where we’re meeting, what order we’re doing things in, that kind of thing — and I’ll be looking at them, nodding, really trying to be present.

But then suddenly I realize I’ve lost the middle part of what they said. I caught the beginning, and then maybe I catch the end, but there’s this blank spot in between. So I have to say, “I’m sorry, can you run that by me again?” And it’s embarrassing, because from their side I’m sure it looks like I wasn’t listening, even though I was trying to.
Do you often feel restless or fidgety?

Restless or fidgety… I’m not completely sure how to answer that. I wouldn’t say I’m bouncing off the walls or anything like that. I don’t think people would look at me and say, “He can’t sit still.”

I mean, I might shift around in a chair, or move my hands a bit, but I’ve always thought of that as pretty normal, especially if I’m sitting for a long time. It’s not something I’ve really noticed as a big problem, and nobody’s pointed it out to me the way they have with the listening or reading things. So… maybe a little here and there, but not in a way that stands out to me.
When this happens, do you usually notice that you’re worrying about something else at the same time?

I’m not sure, honestly. I mean, sometimes I probably am thinking about something else, but I wouldn’t say I’ve clearly noticed, “Oh, I lost the thread because I was worrying.” It doesn’t always feel like worry to me.

A lot of the time it’s more like my mind just… slips off the conversation for a moment. Not necessarily onto some big concern or problem. Sometimes I don’t even know where it went until I realize I missed something. Then I’m more worried afterward, because I’m thinking, “Oh no, what did they just say?” or “Do I have to ask them again?” But I don’t know that worry is usually what starts it.

So I guess the best answer is: I haven’t really noticed that it’s tied to worrying, at least not in any consistent way.
Do these attention lapses cause problems for you with everyday responsibilities, like work tasks, appointments, or paying bills on time?

Yes… mostly with the museum responsibilities, I’d say. I’m not working now, so I don’t have a job where someone is tracking my performance every day, but the museum group has definitely been affected.

I used to feel pretty confident leading the art walks and helping with the planning — remembering who was doing what, where we were meeting, little details like that. And over time, I’ve noticed they’ve sort of… quietly shifted some of those planning pieces away from me. Nobody made a big announcement or anything, and they’ve been kind about it, but I can tell. Someone else will handle the schedule, or the order of things, or make sure the details are written down and followed up on.

And honestly, I don’t blame them, because I haven’t felt as steady with it as I used to. I’ll worry that I’m going to miss something important or mix up part of the plan, so I’ve stopped feeling as confident leading the art walks the way I once did. That bothers me, because it was something I took pride in.
Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?

Down or depressed… I don’t know that I’d put it that strongly. I mean, I have moments where I feel discouraged, especially when I notice I’m not keeping up with things the way I used to, and that can sit with me for a bit. But lately, I wouldn’t say I’ve been walking around feeling depressed all the time.

It’s more like… frustration, maybe embarrassment sometimes. I’ll think, “Why was that so hard?” or “Why did I forget that?” And then I can get a little low about it. But I don’t know if that’s the same as being depressed. I still have good parts of the day, and I don’t feel like everything is hopeless or anything like that.

So I guess my answer would be: not really depressed, no. More bothered by certain things, if that makes sense.
Do you spend a lot of your day worrying about different things?

I don’t think so, not a lot of the day. I mean, I do worry about things here and there, like anybody does, especially if I feel like I’ve dropped the ball on something or I’m not sure I remembered something correctly. Then I might turn it over in my head for a while.

But if you mean am I constantly going from one worry to the next all day long, I don’t think that’s really what’s happening. It’s not like I wake up and spend the whole day anxious about bills, health, family, the future, all stacked up. It’s more occasional, and usually tied to something specific that just happened or something I’m unsure about.

I guess I’d say I can get concerned, maybe overthink certain moments, but I wouldn’t describe myself as worrying all day about lots of different things.
Do you have trouble understanding what people are saying when there’s background noise, like in a crowded room?

I’m not really sure, to be honest. I haven’t especially noticed that as a separate problem. I mean, in a noisy room, I think most people have to lean in a bit or ask someone to repeat themselves, and I probably do that sometimes too, but I can’t say it stands out to me as something that happens a lot or causes trouble.

If I’m at a busy gathering or somewhere with a lot of chatter, I may lose the thread now and then, but I don’t know whether that’s because of the noise, or just because there’s a lot going on. I haven’t thought of it as, “Oh, I can’t understand people when there’s background noise,” if that makes sense. So… no, not that I’ve clearly noticed.
Have these attention problems gotten worse over time?

I’d say yes, or at least they became harder to ignore. It’s not like I woke up one day and everything was suddenly different, but looking back, it’s been causing noticeable trouble for about two years and… maybe four months now.

That was around the time my friend died. He and I had been involved with the museum liaison duties, and after he passed, I ended up taking that over by myself. And I think that’s when I started really noticing that my attention problems were getting in the way more. Before that, maybe I had little lapses or I’d misplace things or lose track, but it didn’t feel like it was creating the same kind of problem. Once I was handling it alone, there was just more to keep straight, and it became more obvious.

So I don’t know if the problems themselves got worse exactly, or if the situation made them stand out more, but since then—since taking on those duties alone—it’s definitely been more noticeable and troublesome.
Do you often lose or misplace things you need, like keys, papers, or your phone?

Yes, that does happen. Probably more than I’d like to admit.

It’s usually not big dramatic things, but the stuff I need right then. Like with the museum things, I’ll put down the camera battery, or the name tags, or an envelope with sign-up sheets in it, and I’ll think, “I’ll put this somewhere safe so I don’t lose it.” And then, of course, that “safe” place disappears from my mind completely.

Then I end up spending half the morning retracing my steps, checking the same table twice, looking in a bag I already looked in, asking myself where I was standing when I last had it. It’s frustrating because I know I had the thing, and I know I put it down intentionally, but I can’t seem to pull up where.

So yes, I do misplace things I need. It’s not every single minute, but it’s often enough that it wastes time and makes me feel kind of foolish.
Do you often need to turn the television or radio up louder than other people prefer?

No, I don’t think so. At least, nobody’s really complained to me that I have the television or radio too loud.

I mean, I suppose sometimes I turn it up a little if there’s noise outside or if the program has quiet dialogue, but I think most people do that. I haven’t had people saying, “Can you turn that down?” or acting like it’s much louder than they can tolerate. So I wouldn’t say that’s been a noticeable problem for me.
Outside of the museum, have you had these same attention problems throughout your adult life?

Yes… yes, I think so. I mean, it wasn’t just the museum, if I’m being honest. The museum made it harder to overlook, but when I think back, this has kind of followed me for a long time.

Even when I was a kid in grade school, my report cards would say things like “daydreams” or “needs reminders to finish work.” I remember that because my mother would get frustrated but also try to help, and she’d sit beside me while I did homework to keep me moving along. That was before I was twelve, so it goes pretty far back.

So outside of the museum, yes, I’d say these kinds of attention problems were there earlier in life too. Maybe I managed around them better at times, or other people helped keep me on track, but it wasn’t brand new.
Have these attention problems caused trouble for you in managing household chores?

Yes, it has, though I notice it maybe in a similar way to the volunteer things more than anything. If I’m given a few steps to handle, I can start out fine and then somehow not carry it all the way through.

Like with the volunteer group, someone might say, “Can you print the maps, call the museum desk, and get the folders ready?” And I’ll print the maps, because that’s the first thing in front of me, and I’ll feel like I’m on top of it. But then the calling part just slips away, or I’ll leave the folders partly done on the table and not realize until someone asks, “Did those get finished?” Then I feel bad because it isn’t that I didn’t care or refused to do it. I honestly meant to finish the whole thing.

At home it can be like that too with chores—if there are several pieces to something, I may do the first part and then leave the rest hanging unless I get reminded or see it sitting there later. It’s not that I can’t do the chore physically. It’s more that the follow-through gets spotty when there’s more than one step.

I mean, in a noisy room, I think most people have to lean in a bit or ask someone to repeat themselves, and I probably do that sometimes too, but I can’t say it stands out to me as something that happens a lot or causes trouble.

If I’m at a busy gathering or somewhere with a lot of chatter, I may lose the thread now and then, but I don’t know whether that’s because of the noise, or just because there’s a lot going on. I haven’t thought of it as, “Oh, I can’t understand people when there’s background noise,” if that makes sense. So… no, not that I’ve clearly noticed.

doctor.intent: Differentiate lifelong ADHD-related inattention from a possible acquired cognitive problem by checking whether the patient has noticed a recent worsening compared with his past baseline.
doctor.question: Have these attention problems gotten worse over time?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: It’s been noticeably causing trouble for about two years and four months, since my friend died and I took over the museum liaison duties by myself.
target_item.reason: The question asks about the course of the attention problems over time, which is best addressed by the duration/onset timeline item describing when they became noticeably troublesome.

patient.answer:
I’d say yes, or at least they became harder to ignore. It’s not like I woke up one day and everything was suddenly different, but looking back, it’s been causing noticeable trouble for about two years and… maybe four months now.

That was around the time my friend died. He and I had been involved with the museum liaison duties, and after he passed, I ended up taking that over by myself. And I think that’s when I started really noticing that my attention problems were getting in the way more. Before that, maybe I had little lapses or I’d misplace things or lose track, but it didn’t feel like it was creating the same kind of problem. Once I was handling it alone, there was just more to keep straight, and it became more obvious.

So I don’t know if the problems themselves got worse exactly, or if the situation made them stand out more, but since then—since taking on those duties alone—it’s definitely been more noticeable and troublesome.

doctor.intent: Differentiate lifelong ADHD-related inattention from possible hearing impairment by testing for a core ADHD symptom outside auditory processing: frequent loss or misplacement of everyday items.
doctor.question: Do you often lose or misplace things you need, like keys, papers, or your phone?

target_item.name: Losing_Items
target_item.manifestation: I’m always putting down the camera battery, name tags, or the envelope with sign-up sheets somewhere safe and then spending half the morning retracing my steps to find them.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether the patient often loses or misplaces needed items such as keys, papers, or a phone, which matches the Losing_Items symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yes, that does happen. Probably more than I’d like to admit.

It’s usually not big dramatic things, but the stuff I need right then. Like with the museum things, I’ll put down the camera battery, or the name tags, or an envelope with sign-up sheets in it, and I’ll think, “I’ll put this somewhere safe so I don’t lose it.” And then, of course, that “safe” place disappears from my mind completely.

Then I end up spending half the morning retracing my steps, checking the same table twice, looking in a bag I already looked in, asking myself where I was standing when I last had it. It’s frustrating because I know I had the thing, and I know I put it down intentionally, but I can’t seem to pull up where.

So yes, I do misplace things I need. It’s not every single minute, but it’s often enough that it wastes time and makes me feel kind of foolish.

doctor.intent: Differentiate lifelong inattentive ADHD from hearing impairment by checking for a hallmark hearing-loss sign the patient may not have volunteered.
doctor.question: Do you often need to turn the television or radio up louder than other people prefer?

target_item.reason: The question is about possible hearing difficulty or needing higher audio volume, which is not covered by the ADHD inattentive symptom profiles provided.

patient.answer:
No, I don’t think so. At least, nobody’s really complained to me that I have the television or radio too loud.

I mean, I suppose sometimes I turn it up a little if there’s noise outside or if the program has quiet dialogue, but I think most people do that. I haven’t had people saying, “Can you turn that down?” or acting like it’s much louder than they can tolerate. So I wouldn’t say that’s been a noticeable problem for me.

inference.note: Removed H91.90: patient denies signs suggestive of hearing loss (no muffled hearing, no need for louder TV/radio, no clear difficulty in background noise). Persistent childhood-onset inattention with distractibility and misplacing items supports ADHD/inattention over primary hearing disorder.

doctor.intent: Differentiate lifelong ADHD-related inattentiveness from an unspecified recent concentration problem by confirming whether the symptoms have been present across multiple settings throughout adulthood, not just during the museum role.
doctor.question: Outside of the museum, have you had these same attention problems throughout your adult life?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even back in grade school, my report cards said things like “daydreams” and “needs reminders to finish work,” and my mother used to sit beside me to keep me on track with homework before I was twelve.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the attention problems have been longstanding beyond the current museum situation, which most directly relates to the history of symptoms beginning earlier in life.

patient.answer:
Yes… yes, I think so. I mean, it wasn’t just the museum, if I’m being honest. The museum made it harder to overlook, but when I think back, this has kind of followed me for a long time.

Even when I was a kid in grade school, my report cards would say things like “daydreams” or “needs reminders to finish work.” I remember that because my mother would get frustrated but also try to help, and she’d sit beside me while I did homework to keep me moving along. That was before I was twelve, so it goes pretty far back.

So outside of the museum, yes, I’d say these kinds of attention problems were there earlier in life too. Maybe I managed around them better at times, or other people helped keep me on track, but it wasn’t brand new.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the attention problem reflects ADHD-level impairment across another adult life domain beyond the museum, helping distinguish ADHD from a nonspecific concentration complaint.
doctor.question: Have these attention problems caused trouble for you in managing household chores?

target_item.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: When someone gives me a few things to handle for the volunteer group, I’ll do the first part, like printing the maps, but then I may forget to call the museum desk or leave the folders half-ready until someone reminds me.
target_item.reason: The question is specifically about whether attention problems interfere with completing or managing chores, which matches difficulty following through and finishing chores or duties.

patient.answer:
Yes, it has, though I notice it maybe in a similar way to the volunteer things more than anything. If I’m given a few steps to handle, I can start out fine and then somehow not carry it all the way through.

Like with the volunteer group, someone might say, “Can you print the maps, call the museum desk, and get the folders ready?” And I’ll print the maps, because that’s the first thing in front of me, and I’ll feel like I’m on top of it. But then the calling part just slips away, or I’ll leave the folders partly done on the table and not realize until someone asks, “Did those get finished?” Then I feel bad because it isn’t that I didn’t care or refused to do it. I honestly meant to finish the whole thing.

At home it can be like that too with chores—if there are several pieces to something, I may do the first part and then leave the rest hanging unless I get reminded or see it sitting there later. It’s not that I can’t do the chore physically. It’s more that the follow-through gets spotty when there’s more than one step.

inference.note: History now clearly supports lifelong, cross-situational inattentive symptoms with functional impairment (childhood onset, adult persistence, disorganization, losing things, poor follow-through), which favors ADHD predominantly inattentive presentation over nonspecific concentration difficulty; hearing, anxiety, and depression explanations were not supported.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking help today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a longstanding pattern of inattentive symptoms beginning in childhood and persisting into adulthood across multiple settings, with clear functional impairment. Confirmed features include losing track during conversations, mind wandering while reading, needing repeated reminders to finish tasks in childhood, misplacing necessary items, and poor follow-through on multistep responsibilities and chores. Onset before age 12 is explicitly confirmed, symptoms occur in more than one setting, and anxiety, depression, and primary hearing problems were not supported as better explanations. Hyperactive-impulsive symptoms are not prominent, supporting ADHD predominantly inattentive presentation.
